t: Pythagorean Distance Nodes in a Tree — Three BFS Traversals
o: For every node u we need its distances to three fixed targets x, y, z, and we count u if the sorted triple (a, b, c) satisfies a² + b² = c² (zeros allowed, as in Example 1 where 0,2,2 qualifies). In a tree, distance = level difference, so one BFS/DFS per target gives all distances in O(n). With n up to 1e5 we need linear time; checking each node afterwards is O(1).
k: Three BFS runs from x, y, z give dx, dy, dz for every node in O(n).
The Pythagorean check is on the sorted triple; note 0² + c² = c² so a node coinciding with a target can be special.
Distances fit easily in standard integer types (max distance < n).

a.i: Build the adjacency list once, run BFS from each of the three targets to fill three distance arrays, then test the sorted squared relation at every node.
s: BFS from x, y, z producing dx, dy, dz.
For each node sort its three distances and test a²+b² == c².
a.t: O(n) — three linear traversals plus a linear check
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency list and three distance arrays

w: This is the natural optimal solution; an iterative DFS works identically. Pitfalls: forgetting that a distance of 0 is allowed (targets themselves may be special), and integer overflow of squares in fixed-width languages (distances up to ~1e5 square to ~1e10, so use 64-bit). Follow-up: how would the answer change on a weighted tree (use Dijkstra)?
